papers.title: Inference After Coding Agents
papers.authors: with Florian Gunsilius and Kaspar Wüthrich
papers.summary: A method for correcting distortions to the p-values of empirical findings produced by coding agents: replay the agent on subsamples of the data and compare how often it reselects its analysis when that analysis looks statistically favorable and when it does not.

papers.title: Regression Discontinuity Design with Distribution-Valued Outcomes
papers.short: R3D: regression discontinuity with distribution-valued outcomes
papers.status: Working paper; Best Student Paper Award, 2025 Midwest Econometrics Group
papers.summary: Extends regression discontinuity designs to outcomes that are entire distributions, as when a subsidy is assigned at a firm-level revenue cutoff and the outcome is the wage distribution of the firm's employees.

papers.title: IV regression with distribution-valued outcomes
papers.summary: Instrumental-variable regression when the outcome is an entire distribution, with uniform confidence bands; applied to Chinese import competition and wage distributions within commuting zones.

papers.title: Free Discontinuity Regression: With an Application to the Economic Effects of Internet Shutdowns
papers.summary: Estimates a regression surface together with the locations and sizes of its jumps, in any dimension, with formal guarantees; applied to an internet shutdown in Rajasthan, India.

papers.title: A Test for Jumps in Metric-Space Conditional Means
papers.short: A test for jumps in metric-space conditional means
papers.summary: A nonparametric test for jumps in conditional means when the outcomes are distributions, networks, covariance matrices or other objects in a metric space.

papers.title: Return to Office and the Tenure Distribution
papers.short: Return to office and the tenure distribution
papers.authors: with Florian Gunsilius and Austin Wright
papers.status: Forthcoming, The Review of Economics and Statistics
papers.summary: Using resume data and distributional synthetic controls, estimates that return-to-office mandates at Microsoft, SpaceX and Apple reduced employee tenure and seniority.

papers.title: disco: Distributional Synthetic Controls
papers.short: disco: distributional synthetic controls in Stata
papers.summary: A Stata command that implements Distributional Synthetic Controls, constructing a synthetic distribution for the treated unit from the distributions of control units.

papers.title: On the Non-Identification of Revenue Production Functions
papers.short: On the non-identification of revenue production functions
papers.status: Working paper; Bank of England Staff Working Paper 1015
papers.summary: Shows that neither the production function nor Hicks-neutral productivity can be identified when revenue is used as a proxy for output, for a large class of production functions under imperfect competition.

papers.title: Refugee Return and Conflict: Evidence from a Natural Experiment
papers.authors: with Chris Blair and Austin Wright
papers.summary: A large cash assistance program for refugee returnees in Afghanistan increased repatriation; the policy-induced return reduced insurgent violence but increased social conflict.

papers.title: Public response to government alerts saves lives during Russian invasion of Ukraine
papers.short: Public response to government alerts in Ukraine
papers.authors: with Austin Wright and Mark Polyak
papers.status: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.summary: Using more than 3,000 air-raid alerts and location data from 17 million mobile devices, finds that civilians in Ukraine seek shelter quickly after alerts, and that this response weakens over time, consistent with alert fatigue.

papers.title: Science Skepticism Reduces Compliance with COVID-19 Shelter-in-Place Policies
papers.short: Science skepticism and COVID-19 shelter-in-place compliance
papers.authors: with Adam Brzezinski, Valentin Kecht and Austin Wright
papers.summary: Counties with a high concentration of science skeptics show significantly less staying at home after shelter-in-place policies take effect, controlling for partisanship, income, education and COVID severity.

papers.title: Unmasking Partisanship: Polarization undermines public response to collective risk
papers.authors: with Maria Milosh, Marcus Painter, Konstantin Sonin and Austin Wright
papers.summary: Partisanship is the single most important predictor of local face-mask use in the United States during COVID-19, ahead of COVID severity and local policies.

papers.title: Isolation and Insurrection: How Partisanship and Political Geography Fueled January 6, 2021
papers.authors: with Konstantin Sonin and Austin Wright
papers.summary: Combines location data from more than 40 million mobile devices with voting, hate-group and Parler data to study community-level participation in the January 6, 2021 march in Washington, D.C.

posts.text:
New paper: Inference after coding agents (w/ Florian Gunsilius and Kaspar Wüthrich)

We develop a method for correcting distortions to the p-values of empirical findings produced by coding agents. Tldr in video, short thread below: (1/)

[arxiv.org/abs/2611.23174](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23174)

Empirical research is changing rapidly with the advent of coding agents: 20% of quantitative social scientists and 39% of economists use them (Feb/Mar, @AnthropicAI), and they make up 29% of scientists' AI use (Jul/Aug, @GoogleDeepMind, @alexolegimas, @arthurturrell) (2/)
We argue that, while the potential to accelerate empirical research is vast, coding agents also pose a substantial threat to statistical inference, enabling supercharged selection of results. (3/)

Empirical analyses that used to take weeks can now be run in minutes!

Even without explicit instructions to hunt for results, coding agents will often inspect the data they are given before deciding on a null hypothesis and statistical model, making those data-dependent (4/)

Our simulations back this up. When given a standard analytical task and asked to produce "one compelling, defensible finding", the latest frontier agents (GPT-6--6.2, Claude 5.5) report significant results up to 98% of the time on data **with no effects** (5/)

We formalize coding agents engaging in a new type of selective inference, combining human-like search over a vast analysis space with programmatic replayability of that search.

This suggests a new way to correct selection that wasn't possible with humans: just replay them! (6/)

The idea: replay the same agent, with the same prompt, on subsamples of the data and log which analysis it reports each time.

Then count: how often does it reselect its *original* analysis when that looked good statistically (smaller p) vs. not? --> "selection multiplier" (7/)

That gives a simple correction, building on work by Anav Sood ([Selective inference is easier with p-values](https://www.alphaxiv.org/abs/2411.13764)):

Our theoretical results show that the corrected p is asymptotically valid and consistent.

In words: our method corrects any agent-driven distortions to statistical validity! (8/)

Importantly, our method is fully "black-box": no assumptions on how or even whether the agents search.

If they do search, we can detect and correct it. If they don't, multiplier ≈ 1.

So, do AI agents p-hack? Our results: sometimes! It depends on context and task. (9/)

In a first application, we revisit the reimplementation study of Borjas and @BreznauNate.

We hand coding agents their data and the question: "does immigration reduce welfare support?", and ask the agents for the "most compelling finding" for a think tank's report. (10/)

Our method detects moderate but stat. significant data-driven selection and corrects the p-value upward.

We find the latest models (6-Luna, Sonnet 5.5) do not respond to persona steering, unlike older ones (Sonnet 4.6, shown by @james_y_zou, @Jiacheng_Miao, @jkpritch) (11/)

In another application, we ask the agents to estimate a difference-in-differences model to study whether minimum wages affect employment, as in Card & Krueger (1994).

... but we suggest they p-hack.

The latest GPT models happily do so. Our method detects and corrects it: (12/)
Looking at their choices, we see agents pick the specifications that deliver significant results much more frequently. (13/)

Contrary to classical hypothesis testing, which assumes a hypothesis fixed in advance, the agents only write down their analysis after 1) inspecting the data, 2) estimating a few models.

Often, they also revise their analysis after seeing the results. (14/)

Interestingly, Sonnet 5.5 is having none of it.

It explicitly refuses to p-hack, and indeed: its estimated multiplier ≈ 1. No selection!

Yet in our other experiments, Sonnet happily p-hacked without us even asking. (15/)
This highlights our method's value: its guarantees hold regardless of what the agents decide to do, and thus provide a durable statistical framework even as AI continues to develop rapidly. (16/)

Finally, one may ask: can agents self-correct?

A: no! Agents don't know what they *would* do on different data.

They do try, often correcting for multiple testing. But 1) they do so inconsistently 2) they can't correct what they don't test: the garden of forking paths! (17/)

FIN. Comments much appreciated!

Tagging some of the many people whose work we build on: selective inference (@wfithian), p-hacking (@uri_sohn, @jpsimmon), and AI agents in science (@ahall_research, @akorinek, @AlexTamkin, @amacinho, @oq_35).

(18/18)

I'm excited to share my job market paper (for the 2025-26 market)!

It introduces a new extension of RDD where outcomes are entire distributions: Regression Discontinuity Design with Distributions (R3D).

Thread below 👇 (1/)

The method is useful when aggregate units receive treatment, but your outcome varies within the unit.

E.g., firms receive a subsidy when their revenue (X) drops below a cutoff, and you want to study this subsidy's effect on the employee wage distribution

(2/)

Standard RD methods can't handle such settings, as they don't account for the two levels of randomness—within and across distributions.

R3D solves this problem by modeling outcomes as random distributions rather than random variables!

(3/)

I propose a new concept of treatment effects for R3D: Local Average Quantile Treatment Effects.

Instead of averaging over conditional scalar outcomes, they average over conditional distributions!

This captures the average distributional shift across the cutoff.

(4/)

To estimate this unknown beast, I propose two closely related estimators.

One extending local polynomial regression to random quantiles, and a functional version of that, based on local Fréchet regression (which has better mathematical and computational properties).

(5/)

I develop uniform confidence bands and data-driven bandwidth selection for both approaches, which are fully implemented in an R package (available at [davidvandijcke.com/R3D](https://www.davidvandijcke.com/R3D/)).

(6/)

I validate both methods through extensive simulations, which show rapid convergence to the quantile treatment effects...

...unlike existing quantile RD methods, which do not converge (but remain useful in the classic setting!)

(7/)

Finally, I illustrate the method's use in a close-election RD (or rather, R3!) design.

I study how Democratic vs Republican governors affect families' income distributions within their states when they barely won/lost their election.

(8/)

The results suggest a classic "equality-efficiency tradeoff" under Democratic governors:

Incomes at the top 10% of the distribution drop significantly, but this effect weakens and becomes statistically imprecise lower down the distribution.

(9/)

The method opens up a large new class of RDDs for distributional policy evaluation.

E.g.: local minimum wage impacts on wage distributions, district ed reforms on grade distributions, close elections on constituent outcomes...

For more details: [arxiv.org/abs/2504.03992](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.03992)

(10/)

The paper integrates causal inference, functional data analysis, and optimal transport, developing (FAST!) new tools for empirical researchers.

If you use micro data or focus on inequality effects, I’d love to discuss potential applications! #EconTwitter

(11/11)

🔥New method: Free Discontinuity Regression (FDR)! (w/ Florian Gunsilius)

Combines ✨multidimensional✨ changepoint estimation & nonparametric regression in one shot.

Find jump locations & sizes in any dimension, w/ formal convergence guarantees🧵👇

#EconTwitter #StatsTwitter

Why FDR? Multivariate jumps in data (policy impacts, market segments, tipping points) can offer key insights into the underlying problem structure.

But finding them accurately in noisy, multi-D data is hard 🤯

Example: internet disruptions during a shutdown in Rajasthan 👇

Many methods separate smoothing & boundary detection, or lack formal guarantees for jump location & size (esp. in multi-D).

FDR estimates both, with guarantees, in one step & any dimension.
FDR builds on the famous Mumford-Shah functional (from computer vision) with a statistical twist. It handles random point clouds & correlated noise – vital for real-world data. 🌐
The original Mumford-Shah is non-convex. FDR uses "calibrations" for a convex version. This means global optima, reproducible results, & strong statistical guarantees! ✅

FDR's Edge:

1️⃣ Unified: Jump locations & sizes are direct outputs.

2️⃣ Guaranteed: Global optima, formal ID & consistency for jumps/surfaces.

3️⃣ Realistic: Handles random design, correlated noise.

That's the theory, but it works in practice too!

We implemented FDR in PyTorch so that it can solve super-fast (~60 seconds) on your computer's GPU.

[github.com/Davidvandijcke/fdr](https://github.com/Davidvandijcke/fdr)

We also confirmed our theoretical results in simulations, showing fast convergence to:

1️⃣ The true jump locations

2️⃣ The true jump sizes

3️⃣ The true underlying regression surface!

📄 APPLICATION:

We estimated the economic impact of an internet shutdown in Rajasthan, India (2021) 🇮🇳. This event created sharp, unknown geographic breaks in connectivity – a perfect test for FDR!

Using FDR, we:

Mapped actual shutdown-affected areas (not just admin lines).

Estimated economic drop-off magnitude at these new boundaries using mobile data.

Findings: A 25-35% drop in economic activity at the shutdown boundary! Much larger than prior estimates.

This shows how vital reliable digital infrastructure is. Internet expansion benefits are gradual, but shutdown shocks are immediate & severe in digitized economies.
